{{Short description|Relation between the ionization state of a gas and the temperature and pressure}}
In physics, the '''Saha ionization equation''' is an expression that relates the ionization state of a gas in thermal equilibrium to the temperature and pressure.<ref name="isbn0-521-84735-4">{{cite book |author=Alexander A. Fridman |title=Plasma Chemistry |url=https://archive.org/details/plasmachemistry00frid |url-access=limited |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |location=Cambridge, UK |year=2008 |pages= [https://archive.org/details/plasmachemistry00frid/page/n137 94]|isbn=978-0-521-84735-3 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Chen |first=Francis F. |author-link=Francis F. Chen |url=https://www.springer.com/us/book/9783319223087 |title=Introduction to Plasma Physics and Controlled Fusion |publisher=www.springer.com |year=2016 |isbn=978-3-319-22309-4 |page=2 |bibcode=2016ippc.book.....C |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-22309-4}}</ref> The equation is a result of combining ideas of quantum mechanics and statistical mechanics and is used to explain the spectral classification of stars. The expression was developed by physicist [[Meghnad Saha]] in 1920.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Saha |first1=Megh Nad |year=1920 |title=LIII. Ionization in the solar chromosphere |url=https://zenodo.org/record/1430870 |journal=Philosophical Magazine |series=Series 6 |volume=40 |issue=238 |pages=472–488 |doi=10.1080/14786441008636148}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1098/rspa.1921.0029|title=On a Physical Theory of Stellar Spectra|year=1921|last1=Saha|first1=M. N.|journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society A: Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences|volume=99|issue=697|pages=135–153|bibcode = 1921RSPSA..99..135S |doi-access=free}}</ref> It is discussed in many textbooks on statistical physics and plasma physics.<ref>{{Citation |last=Drake |first=R. Paul |chapter=Properties of High-Energy-Density Plasmas |date=2018 |title=High-Energy-Density Physics: Foundation of Inertial Fusion and Experimental Astrophysics |series=Graduate Texts in Physics |pages=51–114 |editor-last=Drake |editor-first=R Paul |place=Cham |publisher=Springer International Publishing |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-67711-8_3 |isbn=978-3-319-67711-8}}</ref>

== Description ==
For a [[gas]] at a high enough [[temperature]] (here measured in energy units, i.e. keV or J) and/or [[density]], the thermal collisions of the atoms will [[ionization|ionize]] some of the atoms, making an ionized gas. When several or more of the electrons that are normally bound to the atom in orbits around the [[atomic nucleus]] are freed, they form an independent electron gas cloud co-existing with the surrounding gas of atomic ions and neutral atoms. With sufficient ionization, the gas can become the state of matter called [[Plasma (physics)|plasma]].

The Saha equation describes the degree of ionization for any gas in thermal equilibrium as a function of the temperature, density, and ionization energies of the atoms.

For a gas composed of a single atomic species, the Saha equation is written:<math display="block">\frac{n_{i+1}n_\text{e}}{n_i} = \frac{2}{\lambda_\text{th}^{3}} \frac{g_{i+1}}{g_i} \exp\left[-\frac{\varepsilon_{i+1}-\varepsilon_i}{k_\text{B} T}\right]</math>where:
* <math>n_i</math> is the [[number density]] of atoms in the ''i-''th state of ionization, that is with ''i'' electrons removed.
* <math>g_i</math> is the [[Degenerate energy level|degeneracy]] of state for the ''i''-ions.
* <math>\varepsilon_i</math> is the energy required to remove ''i'' electrons from a neutral atom, creating an ''i''-level ion.
* <math>n_\text{e}</math> is the [[electron density]]
* <math>k_\text{B}</math> is the [[Boltzmann constant]]
* <math>\lambda_\text{th}</math> is the [[thermal de Broglie wavelength]] of an electron <math display="block">\lambda_\text{th} \ \stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}\   \frac{h}{\sqrt{2\pi m_\text{e} k_\text{B} T}}</math>
* <math>m_\text{e}</math> is the [[Mass of electron#Properties and behavior|mass of an electron]]
* <math>T</math> is the [[temperature]] of the gas
* <math>h</math> is the [[Planck constant]]

The expression <math display="inline">(\varepsilon_{i+1}-\varepsilon_i)</math> is the energy required to ionize the species from state <math>i</math> to state <math>i+1</math>.<ref>Baring, Matthew G. "ASTR 350: Lecture Notes – Sept 30, 2021." ''Department of Physics and Astronomy, Rice University'', <nowiki>https://www.ruf.rice.edu/~baring/astr350/astr350_2021_lec_0930.pdf</nowiki>. Accessed 4 May 2025</ref><ref>Pettini, Max. "Stellar Structure & Evolution - Lecture 3." ''Institute of Astronomy, University of Cambridge'', <nowiki>https://people.ast.cam.ac.uk/~pettini/Stellar%20Structure%20Evolution/Lecture03.pdf</nowiki>. Accessed 4 May 2025.</ref>

In the case where only one level of ionization is important, we have <math display="inline">n_1=n_\text{e}</math> for H<sup>+</sup>; defining the total density H/H<sup>+</sup> as <math display="inline">n=n_0+n_1,</math> the Saha equation simplifies to:<math display="block">\frac{n_\text{e}^2}{n-n_\text{e}} = \frac{2}{\lambda_\text{th}^3}\frac{g_1}{g_0}\exp\left[\frac{-\varepsilon}{k_\text{B} T}\right]</math>where <math>\varepsilon</math> is the energy of ionization. We can define the degree of ionization <math display="inline">x=n_1/n</math> and find<math display="block">\frac{x^2}{1-x}=A= \frac{2}{n\lambda_\text{th}^3}\frac{g_1}{g_0}\exp\left[\frac{-\varepsilon}{k_\text{B} T}\right]</math>This gives a quadratic equation that can be solved (in closed form):<math display="block">x^2+Ax-A=0, x=(A\sqrt{(1+\tfrac{4}{A})}-A)/2</math>For small <math display="inline">A(T),</math> low temperature, <math display="inline">x\approx A^{1/2},\propto n^{-1/2},</math> so that the ionization decreases with higher number density (factors 10 in both plots).

Note that except for weakly ionized plasmas, the plasma environment affects the atomic structure with the subsequent lowering of the ionization potentials and the "cutoff" of the [[Partition function (statistical mechanics)|partition function]]. Therefore, <math>\varepsilon_i</math> and <math>g_i</math> depend, in general, on <math>T</math> and <math>n_\text{e}</math> and solving the Saha equation is only possible [[Iterative method|iteratively]].
[[File:Saha ionization hyd.svg|frame|Range in temperature equals 0.2 ε/''k''<sub>B</sub> and is 0.30 of ''T'' scale below. Calculated ionization ''x''<sub>H/e</sub> in [[chromosphere]] or at [[Inductively coupled plasma|ICP]] conditions?]]

As a simple example, imagine a gas of monatomic hydrogen, set <math>g_0=g_1</math> and let {{nowrap|1=<math>\varepsilon</math> = {{val|13.6|ul=eV}} ({{val|158,000|u=K}})}}, the [[ionization energy]] of hydrogen from its ground state. Let {{nowrap|1=<math>n</math> = {{val|2.69|e=25|u=m<sup>−3</sup>}}}}, which is the [[Loschmidt constant]] (n''<sub>L</sub>'' for ''N<sub>A</sub>''), or particle density of Earth's atmosphere at standard pressure and temperature. At {{nowrap|1=<math>T</math> = {{val|300|u=K}}}}, the ionization is essentially none: {{nowrap|1=<math>x</math> = {{val|5|e=-115}}}} and there would almost certainly be no ionized atoms in the volume of Earth's atmosphere. But <math>x</math> increases rapidly with <math>T</math>, reaching 0.35 for {{nowrap|1=<math>T</math> = {{val|20,000|u=K}}}}.<ref>Small  <math display="inline">x\approx\sqrt{2/n_L}/\lambda_\text{th}(T)^{3/2}\exp\left[\frac{-\varepsilon}{2k_\text{B}T}\right], \,\propto T^{3/4}/\exp\left[\frac{\epsilon}{2k_B T}\right]</math>10,20,40 10³ K: 0.35÷(2<sup>0.75</sup> e<sup>4</sup>) 91.8 → ''x'' = 0.35 → 0.35 × 12.4? 2<sup>0.75</sup> e²

• If ''x''=0.5=''A'': <math display="inline">4/n=\lambda_\text{th}(k_BT_h)^3 \exp\left[\frac{\varepsilon}{k_\text{B}T_h}\right], \,T_h=f(n)/k_B</math> ''T'' at 50% ionization rising with total ion number density, ''n''. Points of inflection (''T''<sub>in</sub>,''x''<sub>in</sub>) <math display="inline">0<x'(T)={\partial x\over\partial A}{\operatorname{d}\!A\over\operatorname{d}\!T} \,{max.\,at\,T_{in}},\,x''(T_{in})=0</math> depend on ''n/n''<sub>0</sub>.

• x≈0.5(0.38), A=0.25; x≈0.4(0.32), A=0.16; x≈0.3(0.080), A=0.09; x≈0.2(0.18), A=0.04; x≈0.1(0.095), A=0.01;</ref> There is substantial ionization even though this <math display="inline">k_BT</math> is much less than the ionization energy (although this depends somewhat on density). This is a common occurrence. Physically, it stems from the fact that at a given temperature, the particles have a distribution of energies, including some with several times <math display="inline">k_BT.</math> These high energy particles are much more effective at ionizing atoms.

In Earth's atmosphere, [[Kennelly–Heaviside layer|ionization]] is actually governed not by the Saha equation but by very energetic [[cosmic ray]]s, largely of [[muon]]s. These particles are not in thermal equilibrium with the atmosphere, so they are not at its temperature and the Saha logic does not apply.[[File:SahaEquationHydrogen.svg|Ionization of hydrogen from the Saha equation vs. temperature for 3 total ion number densities (relative to the [[Loschmidt constant]] <math display="inline">n_0=p_{atm}/(k_BT_{std})</math>).|none|frame]]
Rigorously, the Saha equation is only valid for dilute gases, due to the underlying [[ideal gas]] assumption used in its derivation. For dense gases this assumption is no longer valid, because particle interactions becoming significant modifies the chemical potential of the species. And the [[Compressibility factor|compressibility]] of ionized gas and plasma. Hence, the Saha ionization framework has been extended to deal with systems that are denser than the ideal gas limit p/[[Gas constant|R]]T [<nowiki/>[[Mole (unit)|mole]]/m<sup>3</sup>], by incorporating corrections for these non-ideal interactions into the [[thermodynamic potential]].<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.108.038302|title = Theory of Thermally Activated Ionization and Dissociation of Bound States|year=2012|last1=Zaccone|first1=Alessio|last2=Terentjev|first2=Eugene M.|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=108| issue=3 |article-number=038302| pmid=22400791 |url=https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.108.038302|arxiv=1202.3306 | bibcode=2012PhRvL.108c8302Z }}</ref> This correction leads to improved estimates for the degree of ionization in the [[Stellar corona|corona]] of the Sun.

== Particle densities ==
The Saha equation is useful for determining the ratio of particle densities for two different ionization levels. The most useful form of the Saha equation for this purpose is<math display="block">\frac{Z_i}{N_i} = \frac{Z_{i+1}Z_e}{N_{i+1}N_e},</math>where ''Z'' denotes the [[partition function (statistical mechanics)|partition function]] of atom/ion resp. electron. The Saha equation can be seen as a restatement of the equilibrium condition for the [[chemical potential]]s:<math display="block">\mu_i = \mu_{i+1} + \mu_e\,</math>

This equation simply states that the potential for an atom of ionization state ''i'' to ionize is the same as the potential for an electron and an atom of ionization state {{nowrap|''i'' + 1}}. The potentials are equal, therefore the system is in equilibrium and no ''net'' change of ionization will occur.

== Stellar atmospheres ==
In the early nineteen-twenties [[Ralph H. Fowler]] (in collaboration with [[Charles Galton Darwin]]) developed a new method in [[statistical mechanics]] permitting a systematic calculation of the equilibrium properties of matter. He used this to provide a rigorous derivation of the ionization formula which Saha had obtained, by extending to the ionization of atoms the theorem of [[Jacobus Henricus van 't Hoff]], used in physical chemistry for its application to molecular dissociation. Also, a significant improvement in the Saha equation introduced by Fowler was to include the effect of the excited states of atoms and ions. A further important step forward came in 1923, when [[Edward Arthur Milne]] and R.H. Fowler published a paper in the ''[[Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society]]'', showing that the criterion of the maximum intensity of absorption lines (belonging to subordinate series of a neutral atom) was much more fruitful in giving information about physical parameters of stellar atmospheres than the criterion employed by Saha which consisted in the marginal appearance or disappearance of absorption lines. The latter criterion requires some knowledge of the relevant pressures in the stellar atmospheres, and Saha following the generally accepted view at the time assumed a value of the order of 1 to 0.1 atmosphere. Milne wrote:
<blockquote>
Saha had concentrated on the marginal appearances and disappearances of absorption lines in the stellar sequence, assuming an order of magnitude for the pressure in a stellar atmosphere and calculating the temperature where increasing ionization, for example, inhibited further absorption of the line in question owing to the loss of the series electron. As Fowler and I were one day stamping round my rooms in Trinity and discussing this, it suddenly occurred to me that the maximum intensity of the [[Balmer series|Balmer lines of hydrogen]], for example, was readily explained by the consideration that at the lower temperatures there were too few excited atoms to give appreciable absorption, whilst at the higher temperatures there are too few neutral atoms left to give any absorption. ... That evening I did a hasty order of magnitude calculation of the effect and found that to agree with a temperature of 10000° [K] for the stars of type A0, where the Balmer lines have their maximum, a pressure of the order of 10<sup>−4</sup> atmosphere was required. This was very exciting, because standard determinations of pressures in stellar atmospheres from line shifts and line widths had been supposed to indicate a pressure of the order of one atmosphere or more, and I had begun on other grounds to disbelieve this.<ref>{{cite web |title=Biographical Memoirs: Meghnad Saha |url=https://www.saha.ac.in/web/founder/founder-life-works?showall=1&limitstart= |website=www.saha.ac.in}}</ref>
</blockquote>

The generally accepted view at the time assumed that the composition of stars were similar to Earth. However, in 1925 [[Cecilia Payne-Gaposchkin|Cecilia Payne]] used Saha's ionization theory to calculate that the composition of stellar atmospheres is as we now know it; mostly hydrogen and helium, expanding the knowledge of stars.<ref name="amnh">{{cite web |author1=Steven Soter |last2=Neil deGrasse Tyson |author-link2=Neil deGrasse Tyson |date=2000 |title=Cecilia Payne and the Composition of the Stars |work=American Museum of Natural History |url=https://www.amnh.org/learn-teach/curriculum-collections/cosmic-horizons-book/cecilia-payne-profile |publisher=[[American Museum of Natural History]]}}</ref>

== Stellar coronae ==
Saha equilibrium prevails when the plasma is in [[Thermodynamic equilibrium#Local and global equilibrium|local thermodynamic equilibrium]], which is not the case in the optically thin [[Stellar corona|corona]]. Here the equilibrium ionization states must be estimated by detailed statistical calculation of collision and recombination rates.

== Early universe ==
Equilibrium ionization, described by the Saha equation, explains evolution in the early universe. After the [[Big Bang]], all atoms were ionized, leaving mostly protons and electrons (looking in the past). According to Saha's approach, when the universe had expanded and cooled such that the temperature reached about {{val|3,000|u=K}}, electrons (re)combined with protons (10 [[Femtometre|fm]]) forming [[hydrogen]] atoms (0.1&nbsp;nm). At this point, 700 millennia since it was 100 million K, the universe became transparent to most electromagnetic radiation. That {{val|3,000|u=K}} surface, red-shifted in time by a factor of about 1,000, generated the 2.7 K [[cosmic microwave background radiation]], which pervades the universe today.
